It centres on entities like EU movers, third-country nationals (TCNs), domestic workers, and healthcare professionals, with figures such as 27% of EU movers at risk of poverty, 19% housing cost overburden, and 54 hours weekly work for live-in domestic workers. The community also references the Adult Education Survey, ALMA, and the Affordable Housing Initiative, alongside time periods like 2019Q4–2024Q2.

summaries.text: This community centres on the **2024 Annual Report on Intra-EU Labour Mobility**, analysing worker movement across EU and EFTA countries for 2022–2023. Main themes include **mobility flows and stocks**, **cross-border workers**, **postings**, and **socio-demographic characteristics** of working-age movers (20–64 years). Key entities are **EU-27**, **EFTA**, **EU-LFS**, **Eurostat**, **EPSR**, and **EURES**, with specific data points like **13.9 million long-term movers**, **10.1 million working-age movers**, **1.83 million cross-border workers**, and **5.5 million postings**. Pages p5–p9 define terms (e.g., “Active,” “Cross-border worker”) and list country codes; p13 presents headline indicators; p18 outlines the report’s aim; p20–p22 explain data sources and previous topics; p28 covers outflows (e.g., 543,000 EU movers in 2022); p30–p32 detail inflows by country, highlighting Germany (241,000), Spain (148,000), and Switzerland (86,000), plus return mobility and TCN inflows (e.g., Ukrainians to Czechia). The community is statistical, policy-oriented, and focused on quantifying labour mobility patterns.

summaries.text:
This community focuses on **future-oriented occupations** in the EU, particularly those impacted by the green and digital transitions, labour shortages, and AI exposure. It also examines **intra-EU labour mobility** among healthcare workers, including returnees.

**Main themes** include the classification of occupations by digital skills intensity (e.g., GDDI, GEDI, LST-D), gender segregation in shortage occupations, and the ageing workforce in healthcare. Key entities are **EWCTS**, **EU-LFS**, **AIOE** (AI occupational exposure), and specific occupation groups like **LST LSF GNE**.

**Key numbers** show that 28% of current jobs are exposed to AI, and the share of EU healthcare movers aged 45+ rose from 51% (2017) to 62% (2023). Returnees accounted for 3% of healthcare workers in Spain and 8% in Sweden.

**Page distribution**: The *future-oriented_occupations* pages (p5–p45) cover occupation classification, AI exposure, and workforce demographics. The *annual_report_on_intra-eu_labour_mobility* pages (p17–p195) detail healthcare worker ageing, contract types, and returnee statistics.

This community covers labour market analysis in Europe, focusing on activity rates, employment and demographic breakdowns by gender and age. Its main themes are the labour market participation of older people (aged 55–64), gender differences in employment, and the situation of EU movers and third-country nationals. The statistical annex pages (labour_market_and_wage_developments_in_europe, pages 110–138) present country-by-country tables of population, labour force, activity rates for young, prime-age and older workers, and male/female splits. Page 89 discusses digital skills of older people and their skills matching, using the Digital Skills Indicator. The annual report pages (146, 181–186) cover EU movers by gender, employment rates of male and female movers, part-time and fixed-term work, and health workers. Key entities include Activity, Employed, Female, Male, Older, Prime, Young, Temporary, Manufacturing, Services, Agriculture, and the projection of future labour market activity.

summaries.text: This community is the 2024 Annual Report of the European Network of Public Employment Services (PES), covering its 10th anniversary year. Main themes include addressing complex labour market challenges, benchmarking for PES modernisation, and looking ahead. Key topics: anticipating labour market needs and skills development; career guidance and Individual Learning Accounts (ILAs); green skills and jobs; attracting skilled labour from third countries; improving service delivery for those furthest from the labour market (NEETs, women caregivers, older jobseekers, persons with disabilities); digitalisation, AI and the AI Act; and governance, including Chair Caroline Mancel (Brussels PES, Actiris) and Board meetings in Liège and Budapest. Numbers cited include the 5.9% EU27 unemployment rate (September 2024), 87% (27 of 31) of PES involved in career guidance, and 71% delivering skills assessments. Pages 4–7 cover introduction, foreword and governance; pages 8–14 cover labour market challenges, skills intelligence, ILAs, green transition and international recruitment; pages 15–23 cover service delivery and performance; pages 24–30 cover benchmarking and outlook.

summaries.text: This community focuses on the access of domestic workers to labour and social protection, specifically in seven non-EU countries: Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Serbia, Kosovo, and Moldova. Key entities include the International Labour Organization Convention C189, the European Social Policy Analysis Network (ESPAN), and various national strategies like the Programme for Combating the Informal Economy of Montenegro. Numbers centre on the estimated share of domestic workers among all workers (e.g., 2.5% in Kosovo, 0.5% in Albania) and demographic data, such as 70% of domestic workers in Moldova being aged 35–54. Pages p8–p12 introduce the report’s scope and definitions. Pages p73–p81 detail the seven countries’ legal frameworks, collective agreements, and undeclared work challenges, while p83–p96 continue with formalisation measures and specific country initiatives.

summaries.text: This community consists of publications from the European Commission’s Directorate-General for Employment, Social Affairs and Inclusion, produced by its analysis and statistics units (Analysis Unit F, F4, and related teams) and the Joint Research Centre. The main themes are EU labour market and social developments: intra-EU labour mobility, free movement of workers, posting of workers, access for domestic workers to labour and social protection, future-oriented occupations, labour market transitions and skills investment, wage developments, and public employment services. The pages centre on front matter—legal notices, contact details, ISBNs and DOIs—rather than substantive analysis. The annual report on intra-EU labour mobility (KE0125029ENN#p4, #p202) covers free movement and social security coordination; future-oriented occupations (KE0125043ENN#p2–3) sits under Directorate F, Unit F4; labour market and wage developments (KEBN24001ENN#p2) under Unit F.2; employment and social developments (KE0125067ENN#p3) credits the Analysis and Statistics Unit. Other pages cover domestic workers’ access to protection, public employment services, and demographic and research perspectives on the future of work. Named contributors include Michela Gasperini, Daniela Cinova, Carly Petracco, Matthew Geraci, Margaux Truc, Giovanni Carletti, Marieke Delanghe and Fabrizio Natale.

This community focuses on the **green transition’s impact on EU labour markets**, particularly the need for worker transitions, skills development, and fair policies to achieve climate neutrality by 2050. The main themes include **labour market transitions** (e.g., workers moving from shrinking sectors like mining to expanding ones like renewable energy), **skills intelligence and training** to address shortages, and the **social and employment dimensions** of climate policies.

Key entities include the **European Climate Law**, **European Green Deal**, **Fit for 55**, **Critical Raw Material Act**, and the **2040 Climate Target Plan**. A central figure is **EUR 520 billion per year** in required investments (2021-2030). Pages like `estimating_labour_market_transitions_and_skills_investment` (p8, p10) detail investment needs and worker flows, while `research_perspectives_on_the_future_of_work` (p12, p13) discuss skills gaps and training programmes. `future-oriented_occupations_in_the_eu` (p11) covers net-positive employment estimates, and `joint_employment_report_2025` (p47) addresses minimum wage reforms and collective bargaining.

This community focuses on policies and practices to improve researchers' careers, working conditions, and gender equality across several European countries. The main themes are: gender equity in academia, tenure-track career paths, open-ended contracts, doctoral reform, work flexibility, return-to-research grants, and employee wellbeing.

Key entities include Germany’s **Federal Programme for Female Professors** and **Joint Federal Government-Länder Tenure Track Programme** (pages 32–33, 39–40),

summaries.text:
This community is a collection of EU contact and information pages appended to various reports on labour, employment, and social issues. Its main theme is providing standardized guidance on how to get in touch with the EU and find official information. The central entities are **Europe Direct** (a service answering questions about the EU), the **Europa website** (for online information in all official languages), **EU Publications** (via op.europa.eu), **EUR-Lex** (for EU law), and the **EU Open Data Portal**.

All 12 pages carry the same core themes: contacting the EU in person at Europe Direct centres, by phone (freephone 00 800 6 7 8 9 10 11 or standard number +32 22999696), or by email/form; finding online information on Europa; accessing EU publications; and consulting EU law on EUR-Lex. Some pages (e.g., *a_demographic_perspective_on_the_future_of_european*, *recruitment_working_conditions_career_development*, *research_perspectives_on_the_future_of_work*, *undeclared_care_work_in_the_eu*) also mention the **EU Open Data Portal**. The community centres on the numbers 15 (entities) and 12 (pages), all of which are identical in their informational purpose.
entities: eu the eu open data portal

summaries.text: This community focuses on EU employment, social investment, and the green transition, with emphasis on fair transitions, skills development, and labour market challenges. Key themes include social protection (especially for domestic workers and undeclared work), social investment returns, housing costs, and workforce adaptation to demographic and technological changes. Central entities include the European Green Deal, Just Transition Mechanism, Net Zero Industry Act, Recovery and Resilience Facility, European Social Fund Plus, and the European Pillar of Social Rights. Prominent figures include 55% GHG reduction by 2030, EUR 44 billion for skills (2021-27), and housing overburden rates (8.8% EU average, 33.5% for at-risk groups). The domestic workers page covers undeclared work and policy instruments; the ESDE pages discuss social investment methods and green transition investments; the labour market transitions page details skills needs and training programs; the JER pages address employment targets, skills gaps, and housing costs; the wage developments page covers the EU Action Plan on labour shortages and the EU Talent Pool.

summaries.text:
This community focuses on **labour market dynamics, sectoral employment, and worker mobility** within the EU, with a strong emphasis on **posting of workers** and **green transition** impacts. The main themes include **sectoral transitions**, **self-employment by sector**, **training and reskilling**, and **material deprivation** among employees.

Key entities centre on **sectors** (Construction, Manufacturing, Transportation, Mining, Agriculture) and **country groups** (BG, DK, IE, DE, FR, RO, MT, HU). Numbers highlight **median ages** in transforming sectors (e.g., 54 in LV Water supply), **shares of self-employment** (e.g., 34% of EU movers in Construction), and **posting volumes** (e.g., 49.5% of DK postings in Transportation).

The pages carry these themes: *annual_report_on_intra-eu_labour_mobility* (p174) details self-employment by sector; *estimating_labour_market_transitions* (p18-19, p41) covers sectoral transitions, training, and median ages; *labour_market_and_wage_developments* (p29, p56) discusses sectoral mismatches and material deprivation; *posting_of_workers* (p35, p48-51) provides detailed posting data by sector and receiving country.

This community centres on undeclared care work in the EU and access for domestic workers to labour and social protection, drawing on a EUROFOUND research paper and a synthesis report. Main themes include policy approaches to formalising undeclared care, the risks care recipients face from unregulated arrangements, and the financial insecurity, fear and exploitation undeclared workers experience. It also covers how formal service availability and affordability shape demand, and instruments such as subsidised domestic work, regularisation of undocumented migrants and professionalisation. Entities include Equinet, FEPS, ELA, the European Care Strategy, and sources such as Pulignano et al, Hrženjak and Janák. Numbers cited include 460,000 people needing care, 91,962 in-home care recipients and 55,686 informal carers. Pages p1, p3, p12, p16, p20, p42, p48 and p50 carry the undeclared care work theme, while p64 addresses domestic workers' access to labour and social protection.

This community focuses on **labour market integration and undeclared care work** in the EU, drawing on two main documents. The first set of pages (p167–p172) from the *Annual Report on Intra-EU Labour Mobility* provides detailed statistical tables on **activity, employment, and unemployment rates** from 2018 to 2023, broken down by nationality group (nationals, EU movers, and third-country nationals) across Member States. Key entities here include **EU-27, AT, BE, DE, IT, and EFTA** countries, with figures showing, for example, that in 2023 the EU-27 employment rate was 76% for nationals, 78% for EU movers, and 63% for TCNs. The second document (p6, p15) from *Undeclared Care Work in the EU* defines abbreviations like **CESU, DLS, INPS, and ISEE**, and estimates **6.8 million undeclared workers** in personal and household services, with **2.1 million in care** and **4.7 million in direct household employment**. The main themes are **labour mobility statistics** and the **scale and characterisation of undeclared care work**.

summaries.text: This community focuses on regional labour market and social indicators across the European Union, primarily drawn from the *Joint Employment Report 2025* and the *Annual Report on Intra-EU Labour Mobility*. The main themes are regional breakdowns of key social scoreboard indicators, including early leavers from education and training (ages 18-24), NEET rates (ages 15-29), employment rates (ages 20-64), unemployment rates (ages 15-74), long-term unemployment, risk of poverty or social exclusion, and unmet needs for medical examination. The community also covers intra-EU labour mobility of health workers by age group (e.g., 24, 29, 59 years). Central entities are NUTS regions (e.g., NUTS1, NUTS2) and specific regions such as Corse, Praga, Zeeland, and Açores, as well as EuroGeographics for administrative boundaries. Pages 155-162 and 164 each present a different indicator map or table, with page 187 providing the health worker mobility data.

This community focuses on **labour market and wage developments in the EU**, with a strong emphasis on **older workers** and the integration of **Ukrainian refugees**. The main themes include promoting labour force participation of older people, addressing ageism, and analysing wage growth and labour shortages.

Key entities include **20Member** (EU states), **Ageing**, **Ageism**, and **Council Directive 2000/78/EC** (equal treatment). The community centres on **4.3 million** temporary protection beneficiaries from Ukraine, with **70%** being women. It also references **over 60%** of Ukrainian refugees having tertiary education.

The themes are distributed across pages: **p7** outlines the report’s structure (labour conditions, wages, older workers). **p25** covers Ukrainian refugee integration. **p42** lists references on labour shortages. **p82** discusses factors influencing older workers’ employment (retirement ages, health). **p97** details training subsidies and wage subsidies for older workers. **p101** lists relevant EU legal acts. **p103** provides references on ageism and low-wage subsidies.

Its main themes are balancing social and employment objectives, skills for a fair green transition, facing digitalisation, inclusivity for vulnerable groups, and recognising gaps in R&I. summaries.text: This community covers poverty, social exclusion and income inequality among EU movers, nationals and third-country nationals (TCNs), drawn from the 2024 Annual Report on Intra-EU Labour Mobility. Its main themes are at-risk-of-poverty-or-social-exclusion (AROPE) rates, at-risk-of-poverty (AROP) rates, severe material and social deprivation (SMSD), very low work intensity, in-work poverty and median income. Key figures include 27% of EU movers at risk of poverty or social exclusion in 2022 versus 19% of nationals and 46% of TCNs, and an EU-27 in-work poverty average of 13%, with Spain’s EU movers at 23%. Pages 82–83 centre on AROPE and AROP by citizenship and country; page 84 on SMSD; page 85 on very low work intensity; page 86 on in-work poverty; and page 98 on median income and the quintile share ratio. Countries such as Spain, Italy, Greece, Portugal, Ireland, Finland and the Netherlands recur as comparisons.

This community focuses on intra-EU labour mobility among healthcare professionals, drawing on the 2024 Annual Report on Intra-EU Labour Mobility. Its main themes are the characteristics, distribution, and working conditions of EU movers compared to national health workers, including gender, age, education, contract types, and return mobility. Key entities include Medical Doctors, Nursing and Midwifery Professionals, Nursing and Midwifery Associate Professionals, and Personal Care Workers, with numbers such as 206,545 EU movers in personal care (4.3% of the workforce) and 4.2 million personal care workers overall.

Page 104 covers EU-mover numbers in healthcare professions and top destinations like Italy. Page 105 outlines research questions and methodology using ISCO-08 categories. Pages 119 and 120 discuss gender and age distributions, noting female relocation trends and ageing movers. Page 122 compares contract types, with 74% of EU movers full-time. Page 123 addresses full-time versus part-time work and return mobility, highlighting Germany as a top returnee destination.

This community focuses on the challenge of **undeclared care and domestic work** in the EU, and the policy measures used to formalise it. The main themes are **prevalence of undeclared work**, **direct versus indirect policy instruments**, and **deterrence**. Central entities include **Care Economy**, **decent work**, **Policymakers**, **Direct** and **Indirect** measures, and **EU’s Gender Equality** strategy. The **ILO Resolution** and **Migration Department** are referenced. The numbers centre on the prevalence of undeclared work in 15 Member States.

Pages from `access_for_domestic_workers` cover the high proportion of **undeclared work** in domestic work (p.60) and call for **Policymakers** to use enhanced data-sharing for formalisation (p.92). Pages from `undeclared_care_work_in_the_eu` define **direct** and **indirect** care (p.11), discuss **deterrence** and preventative approaches (p.31), and contrast **direct** measures (e.g. penalties) with **indirect** measures (e.g. changing norms) (p.32). Page p.10 introduces the **Care Economy** and the **EU’s Gender Equality Strategy**.

This community focuses on European employment, social developments, and labour market policies, with a strong emphasis on social protection expenditure and housing affordability. Key themes include the composition of social benefit spending (old age, sickness, healthcare, family, disability, unemployment, social exclusion, and housing), non-take-up of benefits (e.g., 58% in Spain, 38.5% in Italy, 46.6% in Belgium), and housing costs versus house price increases (2014–2023). Entities referenced include Eurostat, JRC, CEPS, and authors like Akenji, Almeida, and Arundel.

The page on demographic perspective (KJ0125152ENN#p20) introduces the JRC’s science-for-policy role. The main employment chapter (KEBD24002ENN#p29) details social protection expenditure and benefit non-take-up. The social investment chapter (KEBD24002ENN#p89) covers housing policies and affordability trends. The references page (KEBD24002ENN#p103) lists academic sources on minimum income, school closures, and homeownership. The labour market review (KEBN24001ENN#p1) provides the annual overview title.

summaries.text: This community focuses on the labour market impacts of the green transition, particularly the need for skills investment and workforce re-training. The main themes include gender disparities in energy and mining sectors, training participation rates across EU Member States, and projected job creation from renewable energy deployment. Key entities include the Fair Transitions Working Papers, IRENA, IEA, and authors such as Fragkos, Paroussos, García-León, and Kuokkanen. Numerical data centres on gender composition (e.g., women making up 26.7% of the energy workforce in 2023) and training rates (e.g., over 24% in Finland vs. under 5% in Bulgaria). Page 15 covers gender gaps in mining and energy. Page 20 discusses training participation and introduces energy-intensive industries. Page 28 provides a table of projected additional skilled workers and re-training costs for wind and solar by 2030. Page 34 addresses vulnerable regions and green job quality. Page 38 lists references, including studies on employment creation and heatwave impacts.

This community focuses on the challenges and policy responses surrounding undeclared care and domestic work in the EU, particularly for migrant workers. Key themes include the prevalence of informal employment, exploitation risks, and barriers to labour and social protection. It highlights the profile of workers—mostly women and migrants from non-EU countries (e.g., Albania, Bangladesh, Nepal, Philippines, Sri Lanka, Viet Nam)—and the difficulties in enforcing rights due to low unionisation and collective bargaining (e.g., Tarifverträge, Betriebsvereinbarungen). Policy tools discussed include voucher schemes, the RUT system, and legal frameworks like Lithuania’s Law on Social Services and Denmark’s EU Care Pass. The pages cover: p47 on undeclared work and exploitation risks; p59 on collective bargaining and information barriers; p17 on worker profiles and vulnerabilities; p38 on voucher schemes and legal amendments; p44 on future policy actions, including skill frameworks and certification harmonisation.

This community is about estimating the labour market transitions and skills investment needs of the green transition, specifically the additional jobs and re-training costs from wind and solar deployment needed to meet European Green Deal 2030 targets. Its main themes are a step-by-step calculation methodology, investment and job estimates, and sectoral labour mobility. The entities centre on formulas and variables such as AddCap, CAPEX, INV, LABSH, LAB, AvgWage and Jobs, alongside data sources and models including ENTSO-E capacity data, the EU 2020 Reference scenario, JRC GEM E3, GTAP10, PRIMES and GECO. Key numbers include EUR 1.1–1.4 billion in skills investment by 2030 and 142 billion EUR in average annual power plant investment needs. Pages 24–26 carry the methodology and equations (flowchart, capacity additions, investment, job intensity); page 29 presents the skills investment estimate and job creation figure; page 44 covers outward sectoral mobility using LFS microdata.

summaries.text: This community focuses on EU labour mobility, social convergence, and social investment, drawing from four pages of two reports. The main themes are: intra-EU labour mobility (annual report page 12), social convergence and reducing economic disparity (page 36), and the role of social investment in growth and inclusion (page 67). This community is about estimating the labour market transitions and skills investment needs of the green transition, drawing on a working paper (KE0125066ENN). Its main themes are sectoral employment shifts under the European Green Deal and “Fit for 55”, the vulnerability of workers in high-emission industries, and the re-skilling and up-skilling needed to support sustainable employment outcomes. It centres on NACE sectors (B, D, Division, F), “transforming sectors”, and references such as the GTAP Data Base, Causa et al. (2024), CEDEFOP, Eurofound and the OECD. Page 11 discusses expected employment increases in water supply, waste management, construction and trade, and decreases in coke, petroleum, gas and mining. Page 13 presents figures on EU27 employment by NACE sector (2023) and the share of workers in transforming sectors per Member State (2022). Page 22 covers displacement risks, noting 20% higher odds of unemployment for high-carbon jobs. Page 35 is the references list (Aguiar, Ari, Artuç, Cardi, Restout, and others).

summaries.text: This community is a synthesis report on access for domestic workers to labour and social protection, drawing on national reports from 34 ESPAN country teams and on ECE work covering the 27 EU Member States. Its main themes are mapping and estimating the number of domestic workers and their socio-demographic and job characteristics; the legal framework and employment arrangements applying to them; and the formalisation of undeclared work, including through the European Platform tackling undeclared work and six types of national instruments (three direct: monitoring and sanctions, voucher systems, tax incentives). It also flags data limitations: LFS data may underestimate migrants and undeclared workers, so actual domestic worker numbers are likely much higher. Page 10 introduces the report's structure and Part A; page 24 discusses data under-estimation of migrants and undeclared workers; page 62 covers ELA, the Platform and formalisation instruments; page 97 is Annex B, the references list (Baga, Cylus, Rand, Rossow, Bakirtzi, Decker, Lebrun and others).

This community focuses on European employment, social developments, and labour market analysis, drawing on EU policy documents and research. Its main themes include sustainable growth, social mobility, the twin green and digital transitions, and the need for fair transitions for workers in affected industries. It centres on entities like the Social Protection Performance Monitor (SPPM), the Employment and Social Developments in Europe reports, and the Strategic Foresight Report, alongside concepts such as business cycle indicators, integrated social assistance schemes, and returns on investment in education.

The pages carry distinct themes: the 2025 quarterly review (employment_and_social_developments_in_europe-KE0125067ENN#p1) introduces the series. The 2024 report (employment_and_social_developments_in_europe_2024-KEBD24002ENN#p106) lists references on educational achievement, social assistance, and foresight. The labour market page (labour_market_and_wage_developments_in_europe-KEBN24001ENN#p41) covers general conditions, skills shortages, and business cycle indicators. The research perspectives page (research_perspectives_on_the_future_of_work-KI0124087ENN#p23) discusses middle-class pressures, social mobility, and the challenges of the twin transitions.

summaries.text: This community focuses on gender equity and career development in academia, particularly the persistent underrepresentation of women in senior research roles despite decades of policy efforts. Key themes include the insufficiency of “positive action” versus the controversial shift toward “positive discrimination” (e.g., female-only posts, the Programme for Female Professors), and the comparison between Western and Eastern European female researcher shares (EU-average ~41% in STEM). It also examines tenure track models (citing KU Leuven, University of Vienna, University of Copenhagen, Flemish Community) as tools for smoother transitions, alongside challenges like rigid performance targets, competitive salaries, and career breaks due to pregnancy. Entities include Better Place, Irene Curie Fellowship, Senior Academic Leadership Initiative, and SheFigures. Page 13 covers positive action/discrimination and regional disparities; page 17 discusses industry versus academic careers and career breaks; page 24 details tenure track examples and rigidity; page 29 addresses leadership, toxic behaviour, and reasons for leaving academia.

This community focuses on the analysis of income stabilisation and the macroeconomic impact of Cohesion Policy investments, primarily using simulation models. The main themes are the calculation of **Income Stabilisation Coefficients (ISCs)** via the **EUROMOD** model, and the long-term effects of **ESF+** investments on GDP and employment, simulated with a **Computable General Equilibrium (CGE)** model called **RHOMOLO**. Key entities include **DG REGIO**, the **Common Provisions Regulation**, and the **Household Budget Survey**. Numerical results centre on ISC values (e.g., 6.3% in Romania to 45.6% in Denmark for direct taxes) and employment changes (e.g., 40,000 jobs in net receiver regions). Page 94 discusses the composition of income stabilisation by Member State and income quintile. Page 98 describes the CGE simulation of ESF+ investments. Page 100 presents employment simulation results and the analytical method for calculating ISCs. Page 101 shows graphs on consumption footprint inequality (S80/S20 ratio) and ISCs by policy instrument across Member States.

This community focuses on the concept of **underemployment** in the European labour market, distinguishing it from involuntary part-time work. The main themes include the measurement of underemployment, its causes (insufficient labour demand, caring responsibilities, weak bargaining power), and its prevalence across different population groups and sectors. Key entities include **Bell**, **Blanchflower**, **Busilacchi**, **Gallo**, **Luppi**, **Caisl**, **Choi**, **Marinescu**, and **Emerald Publishing Limited**, alongside institutions like the **OECD Economic Outlook** and the **Institutie for Gender Equality**. The community centres on numerical data, such as the finding that underemployment ranges from **12% to 28%** across population groups, and that in countries like **CY, EL, ES, PT**, over **40%** of part-time workers want more hours. Page **#p13** defines underemployment and its importance for labour supply. Page **#p15** discusses cross-country differences and sectoral prevalence. Page **#p16** examines demographic patterns (young, migrant, single, lower-educated workers). Page **#p23** lists academic references supporting the analysis.

This community focuses on the labour and social protection rights of domestic workers, particularly in the European Union. Its main themes are the gaps between formal rights and actual enforcement, the vulnerability of migrant workers, and the prevalence of undeclared or bogus self-employment. Key entities include the **Court of Justice** (with case **C-389/20 CJ v TGSS61**), the **Special Social Security Scheme for Domestic Workers (Sistema Especial)**, and the **Domestic Workers Fund (CAS.SA.COLF)** in Italy. The pages centre on specific national examples: Spain’s recent reforms and the **TGSS** ruling, Italy’s collective agreement benefits, and Austria/Malta’s issues with bogus self-employment. The **marginal earnings threshold** and **marginal part-time** appear as related concepts. Page 16 covers general enforcement and migrant access; page 50 details Spain and Italy’s schemes; page 58 discusses self-employment and co-determination; page 34 (from a different report) broadens to experimental policy interventions for reducing labour market inequalities.
entities: special social security scheme for domestic workers

summaries.text: This community covers European Commission employment and social affairs work, specifically the Directorate-General for Employment, Social Affairs and Inclusion. Its main themes are intra-EU labour mobility, public employment services (PES), posting of workers, fair green and digital transitions, and labour market analysis. The entities centre on Directorate E (Labour Mobility and International Affairs) and its Unit E.1 (Labour Mobility, Public Employment Services, ELA), plus Directorate F's Analysis Unit EMPL F3 (Fair Green and Digital Transitions, Research). Named contacts include Elodie Fazi and A. Fulvimari, with emails for the E1 unit, the PES Secretariat and Fair Transitions. The PES Network, created by a 2014 European Parliament and Council Decision and amended in 2020, is supported financially by the EaSI strand of ESF+ (2021-2027). Page themes: the intra-EU labour mobility annual report and the posting of workers page both carry the Directorate E / Unit E.1 labour mobility and PES theme; the PES Network annual page covers the network, its 2014/2020 legal basis and EaSI funding; the labour market transitions and skills investment page carries the EMPL F3 fair green and digital transitions research theme.

This community is about undeclared care work in the EU, drawing on the report "Undeclared care work in the EU: Policy approaches to a complex socioeconomic challenge." Its main themes are the characterisation and prevalence of undeclared care work, the role of intermediary firms and regulation, and the consequences for workers—financial unsustainability, fear and anxiety (especially during COVID-19), and lack of training opportunities. Page 21 covers characterisation: a Bulgarian EAGLI survey found 3.2% of employers and 12.5% of employees used possibly undeclared goods or services, with household cleaning (15.4%), babysitting and gardening (7.7% each), and 24% paying for care without a contract; Hungarian research links absent legal regulation to undeclared work. Page 28 covers consequences: low or irregular pay (15% of women in Navarre received no holiday remuneration), pandemic vulnerability, and barriers to training. Page 47 is a references list citing sources on Cyprus, Finland, Hungary, Slovenia and Germany (including Minijob-Zentrale on household minijob taxes and deadlines). Entities include Hadjigeorgiou, Mertakka, Harju, Hrženjak, Katona, Melegh and Milánkovics.

This community focuses on European labour market and wage developments, drawing primarily from an annual European Commission review. Its main themes are employment, unemployment, labour force dynamics, and productivity, with a strong emphasis on migration’s role in labour force growth and the impact of digitalisation and automation on jobs. Key entities include the European Commission, Eurostat, the ECB, and the NBER, alongside researchers like Autor, Dorn, and Anderton. The community centres on data from 2010–2023, highlighting a surge in non-EU workers (64.1% of labour force inflows in 2023) and a mismatch index measuring lost hires due to job seeker misallocation. Page 21 covers employment and labour force trends, including migration’s contribution. Page 38 lists academic references on productivity, digitalisation, and automation. Page 45 details the methodology for measuring labour market mismatch and reallocation, using the Sahin et al. (2014) index.

summaries.text: This community is about labour market and wage developments in Europe, with a focus on underemployment, part-time work, minimum wages and productivity. The main themes are the share of part-time workers who want more hours, differences by age and gender, and the policy and research context around minimum income, social dialogue and wage-setting. The entities centre on European Commission publications such as the Annual Sustainable Growth Survey, the Labour Market and Wage Developments annual review, Council recommendations and CELEX legal references, alongside research from Danmarks Nationalbank, Deutsche Bundesbank, DIW and ECB Economic Bulletin. Numbers include the finding that every fifth part-time worker in the EU would like to work more hours, with underemployment about 5 pp lower among middle-aged men, nearly 10 pp among women, and a 13 pp drop for men aged 55-64. The first page carries the underemployment and part-time work theme; the second and third pages carry references on minimum income, minimum wages, productivity and labour disputes.

This community focuses on **employment and social reforms** across EU Member States, with a strong emphasis on **labour protection, social security, and the transition to new working arrangements**. Key themes include strengthening employment protection frameworks, reducing undeclared work, and reforming minimum income and unemployment benefit schemes.

The 44 entities centre on national reforms (e.g., **Croatian Labour Act**, **Czech Labour Code**, **Reddito di Cittadinanza**, **Assegno di Inclusione**), international conventions (**C155**, **C187**), and digital tools (**ARIADNE**). Page **p85** covers Slovenia’s worker consultation rights and civil society involvement in **Territorial Just Transition Plans (TJTPs)**. Page **p86** details Bulgaria’s ratification of ILO conventions, Greece’s **ARIADNE** system, and Italy’s database interoperability. Page **p110** discusses Italy’s replacement of **Reddito di Cittadinanza** with **Assegno di Inclusione** and **Supporto per la Formazione e il Lavoro**, plus France’s reintegration incentives and Poland’s extension of the **ISCRO** scheme for freelancers.

This community centres on the European Social Policy Analysis Network (ESPAN) and its 2024 report, "Access for domestic workers to labour and social protection: An analysis of policies in 34 European countries." The report is authored by Dalila Ghailani, Eric Marlier, Isabel Baptista, Thibaud Deruelle, Ilda Duri, Anne-Catherine Guio, Korina Kominou, Pedro Perista and Slavina Spasova. Pages 1 and 3 carry the title and author theme, identifying the report and its coverage of 34 European countries. Page 99 carries the network-governance theme: Annex C presents the ESPAN network management team and 39 country teams. ESPAN is managed jointly by the Luxembourg Institute of Socio-Economic Research (LISER), the independent research company Applica and the European Social Observatory (OSE). The six-member management team comprises Eric Marlier (ENASSP92 Project Director and ESPAN Coordinator), Anne-Catherine Guio (Deputy Project Director and Co-coordinator), Isabel Baptista (Social Inclusion Leader), Loredana Sementini (MISSOC Coordinator), Slavina Spasova (Social Protection Leader) and Terry Ward (MISSOC Quality Controller). Related entities include the Expert Network for Analytical Support (ENASSP), MISSOC and the Social Observatory.

summaries.text: This community focuses on intra-EU labour mobility, specifically the movement of healthcare workers (doctors and nurses) between EU and EFTA countries, based on the 2024 Annual Report. The main themes are migration flows, net destination/origin countries, and workforce training locations. Key entities include the OECD’s Health Workforce Migration data, national medical associations (e.g., Austrian Medical Association), and countries like Germany, Romania, Italy, Poland, Switzerland, and Norway. Numbers centre on 40,179 EU mover doctors (2017–2022) and 35,784 EU mover nurses, with Germany, Romania, Italy, and Poland providing 47% of doctors, and Switzerland receiving 25% of mobile doctors. Key entities include **65 years**, **8 years**, **Long Term Care**, **Old**, **Ten EU**, and country groupings such as **HU BG LT LV CZ DE** and **LU RO HR SI MT EL**. Central numbers are a 17% projected increase in the EU’s 65+ population, with some countries seeing 20%+ growth (e.g., Luxembourg 39%, Iceland 30%). The page **p108** discusses vacancy rates in human health and social work, and unmet needs rising more for those aged 65+. **p109** details the projected increase in older populations and lists countries with largest growth. **p84** covers inactivity rates of older people, noting the effective labour market exit age (63.8 for men, 63.5 for women) and factors like early exits, care responsibilities, and disabilities.

The main themes are the stability and variation of transition rates across Member States (2010-2019), the influence of worker characteristics (age, gender, career stage) on mobility, and the limitations of the underlying data. Key entities include the EU, individual Member States (e.g., Estonia, Finland, Germany, Romania), and the “transforming sectors” concept. This community focuses on the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on education and employment, alongside broader economic and social research. The main themes are learning losses from school disruptions, gender differences in educational outcomes, and labour market dynamics, including active labour market programmes and macroeconomic modelling. Key entities include Italy, the EU, the JRC, and researchers such as Card, Campos, and Coricelli. The community centres on specific studies, like the analysis of Italian schooling disruptions, and references working papers on regional skills matching and endogenous labour supply.

summaries.text: This community centres on a demographic perspective on the future of European labour force participation, explicitly framed as going “beyond the Draghi report.” Its main themes are the decline of the future EU working-age population, the activation potential of population subgroups, the role of women’s labour force participation, education, migration, and the links between educational composition and GDP growth. The community also covers dynamic projections, the economic impact of ageing, and policy effects on labour supply.

summaries.text: This community focuses on undeclared care work in the EU, drawing on policy reports and references from two pages (p41 and p46). The main themes are the challenges of measuring concealed care work, the cultural context of gender roles, and the growing role of online platforms in both enabling and preventing undeclared work. It centres on European social partner organisations, including EFFAT, EFFE, EFSI, and UNI-Europa, as well as ELA and Eurofound’s NEC. Page p41 carries the core analysis and policy pointers, discussing the individual nature of employers/workers and the normalisation of undeclared care work. Page p46 is primarily a reference list, citing sources such as the PHS Employment Monitor, Eurofound’s COVID-19 working conditions surveys, and the European Commission’s 1998 communication on undeclared work. Together, the pages highlight the socioeconomic complexity and the need for multi-source assessment.

The main themes are EU employment and social policy analysis: the Joint Employment Report 2025 and a report on labour market and wage developments in Europe. The pages centre on institutional roles and named contributors rather than statistics—no figures appear beyond dates such as 31 October. summaries.text: This community focuses on education and workforce reforms, particularly in response to digital and green transitions. A central theme is improving basic skills and teacher training, as seen in the French Community of Belgium’s reforms: extending teacher training from 3 to 4 years (‘Masterisation’), introducing a diagnostic test for French language competences, and gradually reducing the compulsory ECEC age from 4 years and 8 months to 4 years. Another theme is collaboration between industry, universities, and government to address skills shortages, exemplified by Finland’s ‘digitalisation academy’ in the Vaasa region, which partners energy cluster companies with higher education institutions. Key entities include Berghmans, Croatia’s Digital Croatia Strategy, Deutches Schulportal, and the European University Association. The page *joint_employment_report_2025* covers the Belgian teacher training and ECEC reforms, while *research_perspectives_on_the_future_of_work* discusses the Finnish digitalisation academy and broader collaboration dynamics for innovation.

The two pages centre on distinct but complementary themes. The first page, *access_for_domestic_workers_to_labour_and_social_protection*, reports significant labour shortages in domestic work across many EU Member States, particularly in long-term care due to ageing populations. It cites specific predictions: a shortage of 15,000 social and health workers in Denmark by 2035, and demand for helpers in Hungary being twice the actual number. summaries.text: This community covers a two-page section of the Joint Employment Report 2025 on taxation and second earners, especially women, in EU Member States. Its main themes are the inactivity trap and the low-wage trap for second earners, the role of taxation in creating disincentives to work or to increase hours, and related childcare participation. Page 64 centres on childcare: the share of children under three in formal childcare was 37.5% in the EU in 2023, up 1.7 pps from 2022 but below the 2021 level of 37.9% and the revised Barcelona target of 45%; Slovakia (1%) and Czechia (4.4%) had the lowest rates, with Romania (12.3%) and Poland (12.6%) also flagged as a “critical situation.” Page 65 centres on the low-wage trap, noting that around a third (36.6%) of second earners’ incremental earnings are effectively taxed away on average in the EU, and cites Bank estimates of a potential 10% economic gain for Europe from closing gender employment gaps. Entities include Member State codes (LT, SI, DK, LU, BE, DE, RO, PL, FR, HR, HU, PT, CZ, ES, IT, IE) and concepts such as GAPS, Gender Employment Gap and Gendered Taxes.

This community focuses on two main themes: **self-employment patterns among EU movers** and **pension and healthcare reforms** in EU member states. The first theme, drawn from the *Annual Report on Intra-EU Labour Mobility*, examines self-employment by sector, noting that self-employed EU movers are concentrated in construction (34%) and accommodation (12%), while self-employed third-country nationals (TCNs) are also in construction (18%) and accommodation/food services (18%), plus wholesale/retail (26%). Nationals have a more diverse spread across wholesale/retail (15%), professional activities (14%), and agriculture (14%). The second theme, from the *Joint Employment Report 2025*, covers pension age adjustments and healthcare digitalisation. Key entities include **Social Pension Advance (APE Sociale)**, **Option Women**, **Pension Package II**, and the **Digital Act**. Numbers centre on age thresholds: Italy raised the APE Sociale age to 63 years and 5 months, and the Option Women scheme to 61 from 60. Steps to strengthen patient-centred primary care and digital health are also noted, with Germany’s Digital Act and Portugal’s RRP legal acts.

summaries.text: This community focuses on the impact of AI, particularly generative AI and advanced robotics, on the EU labour market. A central theme is the dual nature of these technologies: they offer opportunities for job creation and upskilling, but also pose challenges like job displacement, especially for high-skilled workers, and the rise of an “always-on” culture through telework and digital labour platforms. The EU’s AI Act, which entered into force in August 2024, is a key entity, presented as a framework to ensure AI is trustworthy and safe. Key figures include the fivefold revenue growth of the EU platform economy between 2016 and 2020, and the ILO estimate that over 5% of employment in high-income countries is exposed to generative AI’s automating effects. Page 13 covers active labour market policies, digital platforms, and telework. Page 78 discusses AI’s net employment impact, the potential to replace routine jobs, and the specific risk to high-skilled workers from generative AI.

Its main themes are job creation and local economic development, employers' flexibility requirements, the mismatching of green jobs, decent work, safety and health, and the anticipation of future changes through research and innovation. This community focuses on **student underachievement** in basic skills, particularly in **mathematics** and **reading**, as measured by **PISA Level 2** benchmarks. The main theme is the **rising share of students** failing to reach minimum competence, with data showing increases from 2012 to 2022. Key entities include **PISA**, **OECD**, the **EEA target**, and the **EU’s Digital Education Action Plan**. The community also highlights **policy responses** such as Poland’s curricular reform and Finland’s increased compulsory lessons and funding.

Page 52 centres on the **trend data** (e.g., 30% underachievement in mathematics in 2022) and **national measures** in Poland and Finland. Page 53 expands on **socio-economic disadvantage** (larger learning losses for disadvantaged students during COVID-19) and links to **digital education**, citing the Council’s **Recommendations** under the **Digital Education Action Plan** to support **Europe’s Digital Decade** targets. Both pages reference the **EEA** strategic framework and the need for caution in interpreting 2022 EU values due to sampling issues in several countries.

This community focuses on employee well-being and working conditions, with a strong emphasis on mental health, flexibility, and legal compliance. The main themes are psychosocial risk assessment, work-life balance, and institutional well-being culture. Central entities include **INESC TEC**, **EU OSHA**, the **European Campaign "Safe and healthy work in the digital age 2023-2025"**, and the **Legal Framework for the Promotion of Safety and Health at Work** (Law no. 102/2009). Key numbers are the **4-day week pilot (2023)**, **psychosocial risk analysis surveys (2019; 2024)**, and **periodic occupational gymnastics sessions (2023)**.

Page 19 discusses the national well-being legislation in Portugal, the importance of mental health, and the "unique selling points" of research environments (autonomy, flexibility, academic freedom). Page 44 lists specific measures at INESC TEC, including **flexible** and **hybrid** models, **allocation of additional resting days**, training sessions on mental health, and the work of **Social Responsibility** and **Diversity and Inclusion Committees**. It also notes the institution’s partnership with **EU OSHA** and its compliance with **NP4590** and employer obligations under the **Legal Framework**.

This community focuses on EU labour market and wage developments, especially the labour share of national income and fairness concerns. Page p61 carries that theme: it reports the labour share falling from 63.6% in 2000 to 62.3% in 2017, rising to 62.8% in 2019 and 63.3% in 2020 during COVID-19, then dropping to 61.6% in 2022. It also notes the business profit share averaged 46.2% in 2023–24 versus 45.5% in 2019, raising questions about fair burden-sharing.

Page p75 carries a reference list supporting the wider theme. It cites OECD publications on local economic development, skills for a green and digital transition, artificial intelligence and the labour market, and the net-zero transition. It also includes Pissarides and Arad’s optimistic view on AI and the labour market, plus Riley and Bondibene on minimum wages and firm productivity. Entities such as OECD Skills Outlook, Pissarides, Arad, Riley, and Bondibene appear here. Overall, the community centres on wages, labour costs, labour share, AI, skills, green transitions, and minimum wage effects.

This community centres on a synthesis report titled *Access for domestic workers to labour and social protection*, focusing on the national coordination and expert contributions from Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, and Ukraine. The main themes are social protection, social inclusion, and labour rights for domestic workers. The community lists 24 entities, including researchers such as Evija Kļave, Feliciana Rajevska, and Olga Rajevska (Latvia); Romas Lazutka, Jekaterina Navicke, and Laimutė Žalimiene (Lithuania); Jeff Weitzel, Petra Boewen, and Netty Klein (Luxembourg); and Olga Nikolaieva and Hanna Vakhitova (Ukraine). Affiliated institutions include Vidzeme University of Applied Sciences, Riga Stradins University, Vilnius University, Kyiv School of Economics, and the University of Southern Denmark. Both pages (p107 and p113) carry the same report title and theme of access to labour and social protection for domestic workers, with p107 covering Latvia, Lithuania, and Luxembourg, and p113 covering Ukraine.

This community focuses on **intra-EU labour mobility and wage developments**, centering on the classification and measurement of workers, occupations, and non-compliance with minimum wage rules. The main themes include **occupational categorisation** (using ISCO-1D, ISCO-2D, ISCO-3D, and ISCO-4D), **mobility definitions** (such as "Mover," "Mobile worker," and "Length of stay"), and **wage compliance estimation** (based on EU-SILC and SES data). Key entities include **Active EU EFTA**, **Member the EU**, **Nordic**, **Statebased**, and **Estimations for Germany**. The community also references **Conditions**, **Recitals**, and **MAINSTAT**.

The first page, *annual_report_on_intra-eu_labour_mobility*, covers **ISCO classifications**, **Length of stay**, and definitions of **Mover** and **Mobile worker**. The second page, *labour_market_and_wage_developments_in_europe*, addresses **Estimations of non-compliance** with minimum wages, using **EU-SILC** and **SES** data, and discusses **Wages and labour costs** across EU Member States.

This community focuses on the green transition’s impact on employment, skills, and regional disparities within the EU. The main themes are reskilling and upskilling, unequal distribution of resources across demographics and regions, and the vulnerability of areas dependent on polluting sectors. Key entities include the **Centre for

This community concerns the European Commission’s Annual Review of labour market and wage developments, specifically the general labour market conditions chapter. Its main themes are EU economic stagnation in 2023, the narrow avoidance of recession, the projected recovery in 2024–2025, and labour force participation by citizenship and skill level. It centres on quarterly entities from 2022Q2 to 2024Q2, plus EU Unemployment, Labour Forcenational, Activitysupply, and fragmented heading/table labels such as GENERAL LABOUR MARKET CONDITIONS, MARKET CONDITIONS, GeopoliticalGENERAL, National0, Non EU0, The1, Unemploymentstrong, Upper. Key numbers are GDP growth falling from 3.4% in 2022 to 0.4% in 2023, 0.1% Q3 growth and Q4 stagnation, 0.3% quarterly growth in the first half of 2024, and projected 0.9% in 2024 and 1.5% in 2025. Page p15 carries the macroeconomic and geopolitical-risk narrative; page p22 carries the citizenship/participation analysis and the Table 1.1 quarterly data on unemployment, compensation, and GDP.

This community focuses on labour market and social policy analysis, with a strong emphasis on demographic and attitudinal data. The main themes are the characteristics of domestic workers (age, education, and origin) and public attitudes towards women’s roles in the workplace. Key entities include **Aged**, **foreign-born**, **Germans**, **Religious**, and **Politics**, alongside policy instruments like the **Cohesion Fund** and **Development Fund**. The community centres on specific figures: 46% of domestic workers are aged 50+, 40% have low education (ISCED20 0-2), and 40% are foreign-born. The page *access_for_domestic_workers_to_labour_and_social_protection* carries the worker profile theme, detailing age, education, and nationality splits. The page *employment_and_social_developments_in_europe_2024* covers attitude shifts (1990-2017) by group, including women, the aged, the religious, and those in small towns, measuring changes in views on children, household chores, and job scarcity.

This community focuses on the labour market integration of EU movers, particularly persons with disabilities and young people, as measured against targets in the **ESPR Action Plan** (also referred to as the **EPSR Action Plan**). The main themes are the **employment disability gap** and the **NEET rate** (young people neither in employment nor in education or training).

Key entities include **ESPR**, **ESPR Action Plan**, **F BK**, **FHEM**, **Hid M KcNAB**, **Icg>?e 0CBdcAChe Hid?M**, **PF Icg**, **PF S**, and **TEFd**. Central numbers: a 19% disability prevalence among EU movers (vs. 20% for residents), a 27 percentage point employment gap for movers with disabilities, and a 14% NEET rate for young EU movers (vs. 11% for nationals). The **ESPR Action Plan** sets an 80% employment target and a 9% NEET target by 2030.

Page **#p88** covers the employment disability gap and the **ESPR Action Plan**’s Principle 17. Page **#p95** covers the NEET rate, noting a decrease from 18% in 2017 to 14% in 2022, with country-level variation from 4% (Netherlands) to 26% (Italy).

This community focuses on the **care economy**, defined as both paid and unpaid work for children, the elderly, and other care-dependent groups. It contrasts **declared work** (formally registered, tax-compliant) with **undeclared care work** (lawful activities operating outside official oversight, avoiding tax and social security). Key entities include **Regulated** and **Unregulated** care, **Paid** and **Unpaid** work, **Direct** and **Indirect** care activities, and **Volunteers**. The community also highlights **Profound** societal changes reshaping care work.

Page 7 provides a glossary, defining terms like **Care economy**, **Declared work**, **Direct** and **Indirect care**, **Regulated care**, and **Platform work**. Page 9 introduces the topic, noting that care work is disproportionately done by women, often undervalued, and can be **Regulated** or **Unregulated**. It explains that undeclared care workers avoid tax and social security obligations, and that both trained professionals and non-professionals may engage in this work.

This community is about a European Commission working paper estimating labour market transitions and skills investment needs for the green transition. Its main themes are the transformation of sectors such as energy, mining and quarrying, construction, manufacturing and waste management; net worker inflows into most “transforming sectors” except mining and extraction in the EU; and the unexpected finding that workers in energy-intensive industries make fewer transitions to non-employment than those in other sectors. Possible explanations discussed are higher trade union density and male dominance of these industries, alongside the point that men make relatively fewer employment transitions than women. The community also covers novel estimates of additional workforce and training costs from renewable power generation deployment by 2030, including wind turbines and solar panels needed for EU Green Deal targets. Page 3 carries the abstract and headline findings; page 32 carries the discussion of anecdotal evidence, trade union density, gender differences and the 2030 renewable-deployment cost estimates. Entities centre on JEL codes, J21, J24, J62, Q42, Q47, Černý, Duell, Umweltbundesament and “Anecdotal.”

This community centres on the future of work and the STR Partnership. Page p35 presents broad themes: Europe’s transition to a carbon-neutral economy, human-centric digitalisation, vulnerable groups such as skilled workers in transition industries, and research gaps around future skills, the digital divide, digitalisation/AI impacts, and erosion of social safety nets. It also highlights opportunities in upskilling/reskilling and inclusive education. Page p36 focuses on the STR Partnership: proposed by the Commission in July 2023, one of nine new candidates under the 2025–2027 Horizon Europe strategic plan, aiming for a 7- to 10-year R&I programme using social sciences/humanities to build resilience, fairness, inclusiveness and social cohesion. Its four impact areas include modernising social protection, education/skills, fair climate transition, and shaping the future of work. The partnership may enter the 2026 work programme of cluster 2. Entities: Partnership, Social Transformations, STR, STR Partnership.
